notes: Sample restore_config.json - the backup jobs the toolkit runs, and the restores that prove them. Copy to restore_config.json and edit.

Two lists, and the second is the point. 'backups' takes backups; 'restores' restores them somewhere else and checks the result. A backup nobody has restored is a hope, not a recovery plan, which is why they live in one file and are configured together.

Nothing here names a host or a credential twice: every entry points at db_instances.json by 'server_id' (or by 'id' on a restore's source and target), and the address, container, transport and account are resolved from there. Change a machine in one place.

'env_secrets' maps an environment variable the backup script needs to a key in data/encrypted_secret_text.json. The value is decrypted into the child process's environment and never written to a file or an argument list - an argument is world-readable in the process table.

'jobs' is one entry per backup kind, each with its own schedule and retention, so a full and a log backup of the same database are independent. 'time_window' and 'notify' are the same shared objects used everywhere else.

A restore entry's 'databases' list scopes what is restored. An empty list means 'everything found', which quietly goes on restoring ageing files after a database is removed from the source plan - name them explicitly unless you want that.

'cleanup_retention' is how long a restored copy is kept before it is dropped. A drill target is disposable by design; keeping copies indefinitely fills the target instance and turns a proof into an incident.

A physical restore carries the SOURCE instance's logins and passwords with it. After a drill the target answers to the source's credentials, and the target's own stored credential goes stale - expect that rather than being surprised by it.

Every 'time_window' hour and day bound is read in the timezone DBA Brain runs in - the 'timezone' field in config.json - on every node, whatever clock the host or container keeps. So 'from_hour': 1 is 01:00 there, not 01:00 UTC and not 01:00 on the machine. There is no per-entry timezone: one declaration decides every window in every file. Changing it moves every schedule that names an hour, so set it before the first scheduled run.

space_check: does the incoming copy fit? free >= bytes_to_copy x factor, checked before a share is prepared or a byte is moved. Defaults to on at 1.5 when the entry says nothing. Use 2.0 - as here - when the restored database lands on the same filesystem as its staged backups: the copy is not the only thing that grows, and a restored log file can outgrow anything the backup size predicts. on_unknown says what to do when a number cannot be read; 'refuse' is the default, because an unmeasured restore is the one that fills a disk.

backup_restore._note: Which files are worth copying off a backup share, and how far back to look. A wider window means recopying files that are already there; a narrower one means missing a backup taken late.

backups.note: Full backup of the application instance. The SSH or WinRM transport, the credential and the address all come from db_instances.json via server_id.

jobs._note: A separate job because the log backup is what sets the recovery point objective. Every fifteen minutes, all day - if this schedule and backup_policy.json disagree, the report is right and one of them is wrong.

backups.note: Weekly baseline plus daily incrementals, expressed as TWO jobs: the level is stated in env.BACKUP_LEVEL and the day in time_window.weekdays (ISO 1-7, read on this node's configured clock). The script does not derive a level from the weekday - it used to, reading the container host's clock rather than the node's, which is a different day for part of every day. 'backup_dir' must match the directory the archive metric checks, or a cluster that is backed up daily is reported as never backed up.

jobs._note: Sunday only. Together with the sibling job these cover all seven days exactly once - a gap is a night with no backup, and an overlap is two levels racing for the same night.

Monday to Saturday. Keep repeat_interval well under a day: weekdays says WHICH day and repeat_interval says whether it is due, so a multi-day interval lets the due moment walk past the window and skip whole weeks.

restores.note: The drill. It restores yesterday's backup onto a disposable instance, verifies it, and drops the copy a day later. Scoped to the databases that matter - an empty list would go on restoring whatever it found, including files nobody produces any more. The backups are dbabrain's own and encrypted, so source.backup_certificate reads the certificate pair its backup job exports beside them (from the share, or from source_dir over the source host's login). The drill instance runs in a container on a host with no sqlcmd of its own: target.sql_container runs the container's, and the container binds the import path at the same path.

server_metadata.note: Replays the source instance's server-level metadata - logins, roles, Agent jobs - around the database restore, so the restored databases have no orphaned users. It reads a bundle written by that instance's own backup entry, so turning it on without one only produces a warning every run.
